briefs.summary: This Week at a Glance This week, we explore key trends driving digital transformation across various industries. Organizations are prioritizing technology integration and customer-centric strategies to remain competitive. Understanding these trends i...
briefs.content:
Artificial Intelligence

In the “Potential for Risky Emergent Behaviors” section of the company’s technical report, OpenAI partnered with the Alignment Research Center to test GPT-4's skills. The Center used the AI to convince a human to send the solution to a CAPTCHA code via text message—and it worked.

https://gizmodo.com/gpt4-open-ai-chatbot-task-rabbit-chatgpt-1850227471

Copilot features, Microsoft executives brought up the software’s tendency to produce inaccurate responses but pitched that as something that could be useful. If people realize that Copilot’s responses could be sloppy with the facts, they can edit the inaccuracies and more quickly send their emails or finish their presentation slides.

https://www.cnbc.com/2023/03/16/microsoft-justifies-ais-usefully-wrong-answers.html?__source=sharebar|linkedin&par=sharebar

Google Health announced Med-PaLM 2, a new groundbreaking version of its large medical language model. Med-PaLM 2 consistently performs at an expert level on medical exam questions and reaches an 85% accuracy, scoring 18% higher than its predecessor.

Ubiquitous Compute

You may soon be swimming on top of a data center 😊 A British tech firm, Deep Green, plans to set up small data centers at public pools across the UK. An innovative solution for data center cooling and energy efficiency, this approach uses the excess heat generated by servers installed beneath a public pool to warm the water via a heat exchanger.

The US government has launched a new initiative to help organizations detect security flaws in Microsoft's cloud services. The "Microsoft Cloud Security Technical Reference Architecture" initiative collaborates with the Department of Homeland Security's Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and Microsoft. The program aims to provide organizations with a comprehensive set of guidelines, tools, and best practices to improve the security of their Microsoft cloud services. The initiative is part of a more significant effort by the US government to enhance critical systems and infrastructure cybersecurity.

https://www.techradar.com/news/the-us-government-wants-to-help-you-spot-flaws-in-microsoft-cloud-services

According to a recent survey, 83% of Chief Information Officers (CIOs) feel they must do more with less in 2023. The survey, which polled 500 CIOs in the US and the UK, found that budget constraints are the main factor driving this sentiment, with 74% of respondents citing it as a significant challenge. Additionally, CIOs expressed concerns about the difficulty of finding qualified personnel (55% of respondents) and the need to meet constantly changing business requirements (51%). The survey also found that 87% of CIOs plan to accelerate their adoption of cloud computing this year to help meet their business needs.

https://www.cloudcomputing-news.net/news/2023/mar/13/83-of-cios-must-do-more-with-less-in-2023/

Data Management

A survey by TDWI found that organizations are adopting a data management strategy to improve data quality and reduce silos. 71% of respondents have implemented or planned to implement a data management strategy, but challenges such as data governance and lack of skilled personnel still need to be solved. Organizations are investing in cloud-based data management solutions, master data management, and data integration tools.

https://tdwi.org/articles/2023/03/23/diq-all-data-management-0323.aspx

Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to help solve the problem of IT data overload. IT departments need help managing the sheer volume of data. AI can benefit by analyzing and identifying patterns in large data sets, providing insights that would be difficult to uncover manually. However, AI is not a silver bullet, and organizations must ensure that their data is accurate and high-quality to achieve the full benefits of AI.

https://www.infoworld.com/article/3689668/can-ai-solve-it-s-eternal-data-problem.html

A new report reveals the importance of data management to enterprises. The report highlights how effective data management can help organizations improve decision-making, reduce costs, and comply with regulations. The report recommends that organizations establish a data management strategy, prioritize data quality, and ensure they have the right tools and technologies. The report also stresses the importance of data governance and the need for organizations to foster a culture that values data as a strategic asset.

https://solutionsreview.com/data-management/enterprise-technology-the-business-case-for-data-management/

briefs.summary: This Week at a Glance This week focuses on the critical advances in digital transformation that drive innovation and competitive advantage. Understanding these developments is essential for organizations aiming to remain relevant in a rapidly evolvin...
briefs.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Microsoft confirms new version of its popular AI chatbot will be able to turn text into VIDEO. GPT-4 and future developments will forever change how we think about artificial intelligence. This powerful AI can process text and numbers, videos, images, and more. Microsoft explained that GPT-4 would be “multimodal.” Holger Kenn, Director of Business Strategy at Microsoft Germany, explained that this would allow the company’s AI to translate a user’s text into images, music, and video.

AI to replace actors? Imagine using AI to create a film without hiring real actors or writing a fully illustrated 200-page book in just one day. Yes, you read that right, GPT-4 makes it possible to use artificial intelligence for almost anything you can imagine.

Schrodinger: A ChatGPT-Integrated Fully Interactive Multi-Agent Financial Market Simulator Citadel, one of the world's most successful hedge funds, is in talks to secure an enterprise-wide ChatGPT license. ChatGPT can produce correct code with a (simple) trade execution strategy.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tvzO79V9uq4

Data Management

“Zero” is the new word of the day, with the “Data Alliance” coining the word Zero-Copy for new distributed data architectures. Zero-copy integration is a concept that enables data to be shared between different systems without copying it. The traditional approach of copying data from one system to another can lead to inefficiencies, data consistency issues, and security vulnerabilities.

http://tdan.com/the-data-centric-revolution-zero-copy-integration/30462

The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the vision of data everywhere, in the cloud, the data center, laptops, and IoT devices. This data sprawl has caused IT organizations to re-evaluate their data strategies. New distributed data management strategies and solutions need to be developed that are more comprehensive in managing heterogenous data types, including structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data.

https://www.engineeringnews.co.za/article/modern-data-management-platforms-are-vital-for-solving-modern-data-management-problems-2023-03-14/rep_id:4136

The complexity of data governance is driving organizational changes, including the emergence of the data steward role in organizations. Data stewards are beginning to manage data access, privacy concerns, and data lifecycle management. Placing data stewards in the organization is still up for a healthy debate as organizations mature their data-centric organizations.

https://www.techtarget.com/searchdatamanagement/tip/Data-stewardship-Essential-to-data-governance-strategies

Cybersecurity

An open-source adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing kit has found several takers in the cybercrime world for its ability to orchestrate attacks at scale. Microsoft Threat Intelligence tracks the threat actor behind the kit’s development under its emerging moniker DEV-1101. An AiTM phishing attack typically involves a threat actor attempting to steal and intercept a target's password and session cookies by deploying a proxy server between the user and the website.

https://thehackernews.com/2023/03/microsoft-warns-of-large-scale-use-of.html

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has warned organizations that operate critical infrastructure about ransomware vulnerabilities in their devices. The advisory includes a list of devices that attackers may target and recommends that organizations assess their networks for possible risks. CISA has a newly established Ransomware Vulnerability Warning Pilot (RVWP) program with two goals: to scan critical infrastructure entities' networks and help vulnerable organizations fix the flaws before they get hacked.

https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-now-warns-critical-infrastructure-of-ransomware-vulnerable-devices/

A report by Drata highlights key compliance trends for 2023. The report outlines the shift towards continuous compliance monitoring and the need for automation tools to achieve compliance. It also highlights the increasing focus on privacy regulations and the growing importance of vendor risk management. The report recommends that companies prioritize their compliance efforts, utilize automation tools, and stay current with evolving regulatory requirements to avoid potential fines and reputational damage.

https://drata.com/resources/2023-compliance-trends

Embracing Digital Transformation Podcast

Check out this weeks full length episode "Closing the Digital Skills Gap" where Darren interviews Jon Gottfried from Major League Hacking.

https://www.embracingdigital.org/episode-EDT128

briefs.summary: This Week at a Glance This week presents critical updates on digital transformation strategies across various sectors, focusing on innovation and agility. Understanding these developments is essential for organizations aiming to enhance their operati...
briefs.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Generative AI based Chatbots are far from perfect. ChatGPT, Microsoft's Bing chatbot, Meta's Galactica (a generative AI designed to help scientists with tasks like annotating proteins or writing code), and other systems have been taken down or reined in after they've been found to generate unreliable or incorrect information or spiraled into emotional-seeming reactions and even threats.

The US and European governments are collaborating on an AI research study to develop strategies for regulating and fostering AI innovation. The study will cover five areas: extreme weather and climate forecasting, emergency response management, health and medicine improvements, electric grid optimization, and agriculture optimization. Participants include the US Energy Department, the Department of Agriculture, the Pentagon, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, health and science agencies, and their European counterparts.

https://www.axios.com/2023/03/01/ai-research-us-eu

Airdot Deploy: Automatically deploy ML models and scale them. Automatically identifies the required packages, understands module dependency, re-factors the code, builds REST APIs around the ML model, packages it in a container, spins up the infra, automatically scales it up and down, and sets up automated alerts and monitoring, all with just one line of code. So much for you DevOps team.

https://www.airdot.io/blog/announcing-airdot-deploy-ml

Cybersecurity

A report by Tenable reveals that cyberattacks are primarily carried out using known vulnerabilities for which patches are already available. Threat actors continue to exploit vulnerabilities that organizations have failed to patch or remediate, including high-severity flaws in Microsoft Exchange and virtual private network solutions.

https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2023/03/03/known-exploitable-vulnerabilities/?web_view=true

Municipal CISOs face challenges as cyber threats increase, with ransomware attacks being the largest concern. Oakland, California, recently declared a state of emergency following a ransomware attack by the Playgroup that disrupted phone systems and non-emergency services. This attack is one in a series of ransomware attacks on local governments in the US, including those in Baltimore, New Orleans, Pensacola, and Atlanta.

https://www.csoonline.com/article/3688958/municipal-cisos-grapple-with-challenges-as-cyber-threats-soar.html

President Biden signed the Quantum Computing Cybersecurity Preparedness Act, requiring federal agencies to prioritize using quantum-resistant technology. The law mandates guidance for assessing critical systems with post-quantum cryptography standards. This is in response to fears of quantum technology making existing encryption vulnerable to being cracked quickly.

https://fedscoop.com/biden-signs-quantum-computing-cybersecurity-act-into-law/

Ubiquitous Compute

Accenture's annual banking cloud report found that banks targeting core systems for cloud migration face a major risk factor in the difficulty of sourcing cloud talent. Banks perceive core migration as high-risk due to a lack of staff with cloud expertise and the difficulty of recruiting the required skills in the current environment. Public cloud adoption represents both a security upgrade and a risk factor, reflected in the banking industry's lack of cloud adoption.

https://www.ciodive.com/news/banks-finance-cloud-migration-skils-gap-cybersecurity/644169/

Cloud-based data warehouse company Snowflake plans to add over 1,000 employees in the current fiscal year, according to CFO Mike Scarpelli during the company's Q4 earnings call. This follows the addition of 1,900 people last year, in contrast to the downsizing trend among other big tech companies. Snowflake plans to prioritize hiring in product, engineering, and sales.

https://www.ciodive.com/news/Snowflake-expands-workforce-extends-AWS-partnership/644034/

According to industry experts, CIOs must restructure their IT departments and strategies to take advantage of cloud transformation fully. Neil Holden, CIO at Halfords Group, believes IT departments must operate differently because of the cloud and what it means to the business. Holden reorganized his team to ensure they could maximize the capabilities and business opportunities provided by the cloud.

https://www.cio.com/article/463595/transforming-it-for-cloud-success.html

Embracing Digital Transformation Podcast

Check out this weeks full length episode "Innovation as a Service" where Darren interview Andrew Cohen Managing Director at Netsurit.

https://www.embracingdigital.org/episode-EDT127

briefs.summary: This Week at a Glance This week focuses on the critical advancements in digital transformation across various sectors. Understanding these developments is essential for organizations aiming to enhance efficiency and competitiveness in an increasingly...
briefs.content:
Artificial Intelligence

OpenAI and Bain & Company formed Global AI Services Alliance to transform business potential. Bain will combine its deep digital implementation capabilities and strategic expertise with OpenAI’s AI tools and platforms, including ChatGPT, to help its clients worldwide identify and implement AI's value to maximizing business potential. The Coca-Cola Company is the first company to engage with the new alliance.

Amazon’s cloud unit has partnered with Hugging Face, the maker of ChatGPT rival. Hugging Face will build the next version of its language model, called BLOOM, on AWS.

https://www.seattletimes.com/business/amazons-cloud-unit-partners-with-hugging-face-maker-of-chatgpt-rival/

AI can also be used for actual good in the world too. AI is dreaming up drugs that no one has ever seen. Now we’ve got to see if they work. The first drugs designed with the help of AI are now in clinical trials, the rigorous tests done on human volunteers to see if a treatment is safe—and works—before regulators clear them for widespread use.

https://www.technologyreview.com/2023/02/15/1067904/ai-automation-drug-development

Intelligent Edge

Security vulnerabilities have been found in wireless industrial IoT devices from four vendors, creating a significant attack surface for threat actors looking to exploit operational technology (OT) environments. The flaws offer remote attack entry points, allowing unauthenticated adversaries to gain a foothold and use it as leverage to spread to other hosts, thereby causing serious damage.

https://thehackernews.com/2023/02/critical-infrastructure-at-risk-from.html

The Connectivity Standards Alliance (CSA) has formed a working group dedicated to promoting the adoption of "Matter" for healthcare purposes. Matter is an interoperable standard for smart home devices released by the CSA last year. The Health and Wellness Working Group will align major contributors in the healthcare industry around the Matter standard to ensure secure and interoperable health and wellness devices.

https://www.iottechnews.com/news/2023/feb/10/matter-creator-csa-announces-healthcare-working-group/

Robo-taxis from Amazon’s self-driving vehicle biz Zoox are now on the streets of Foster City, California. Zoox’s vehicles are purpose-built for autonomous driving and do not feature any manual controls. The company’s full-time employees are the first to use the autonomous shuttle service between their campuses. This requires absolute trust in the quality of your team’s work!

https://www.iottechnews.com/news/2023/feb/14/amazon-robotaxis-hit-the-streets-of-california/

Data Management

In a recent study from Informatica on data sprawl, Informatica found that dispersed data and the need for unified management are widespread pain points for many organizations. Additionally, data quality and governance are top priorities. This is leading to increased investment in data technologies this year. The survey-based research found that 78% of CDOs said they must strategically align with revenue-generating organizations to justify the additional spending to improve data analytics and governance.

https://accelerationeconomy.com/data/informatica-research-highlights-data-sprawl-why-management-needs-to-be-unified/

Alation Inc., an enterprise data intelligence solutions provider, has released Alation Marketplaces. This new product allows third-party datasets to augment existing data in the Alation Data Catalog, enabling users to explore external third-party data and supplement existing data sets. In addition, the company has expanded its Alation Anywhere to Microsoft Teams and Alation Connected Sheets to Microsoft Excel to allow data users to access contextual information from the catalog directly within their tool of choice.

https://www.alation.com/press-releases/alation-launches-data-marketplaces/

briefs.summary: This Week at a Glance This week marks significant developments in digital transformation strategies across various sectors. Understanding these advancements is crucial for organizations aiming to enhance their operational efficiency and customer expe...
briefs.content:
Artificial Intelligence

The ethics and regulations of using generative AI-enabled Chatbots are starting to come into play as more people are starting to use ChatGPT and other. Chatbots will now need to include a Warning: We may not produce output that is real. Believe at your own risk. You revoke your right to sue us if you reproduce conversations, images, and videos for high-risk use cases that cause hate, harassment, violence, self-harm, illegal activity, deception, discrimination, or spam.

https://swisscognitive.ch/2023/02/15/honest-lying-why-scaling-generative-ai-responsibly-is-not-a-technology-dilemma-in-as-much-as-a-people-problem/

As AI becomes increasingly important in various industries, the role of Chief AI Officer (CAIO) is emerging as a new addition to the C-Suite. A good CAIO should clearly define the desired impact of AI projects and continuously focus the organization on delivering that outcome. A great CAIO should also track the real impact of those projects and update the business on their performance over time. This role therefore escalates the expectations for driving transformation and impact, as well as anticipating and responding to competitors' use of AI.

https://applieddatascience.medium.com/the-case-for-the-chief-ai-officer-the-newest-c-suite-role-d55cca40c01

IBM’s latest supercomputer is taking several innovative new directions – it is IBM’s first AI-optimized, cloud-native supercomputer, and it is housed entirely within the IBM Cloud rather than on-premises like traditional supercomputers. According to IBM, “this is the go-to environment for IBM Researchers creating most advanced AI capabilities, including work on foundation models and a place where they collaborate with partners on model creation."

https://futurumresearch.com/research-notes/ibms-latest-supercomputer-is-cloud-based-and-ai-focused/

Ubiquitous Compute

According to a study by 451 Research commissioned by Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, almost every cloud journey in enterprises is now becoming a multicloud journey. The study found that 98% of enterprises surveyed are using or plan to use at least two cloud service providers. The top drivers of multicloud strategies are data sovereignty and cost optimization. Enterprises are proactively planning multicloud strategies for the future, with data redundancy being the most anticipated future use case.

https://www.cloudcomputing-news.net/news/2023/feb/21/98-of-firms-using-public-cloud-adopt-multicloud-infrastructure-provider-strategy/

The "supercloud," a cloud architecture that allows seamless migration of applications across different cloud providers, was first proposed by Cornell University researchers in 2016. The concept has resurfaced as a solution to the challenges of multi-cloud, providing a homogeneous network to tie cloud resources together, resulting in seamless migration, consistent security, and optimal performance.

https://www.cloudcomputing-news.net/news/2023/feb/22/here-comes-the-supercloud-what-does-it-mean-for-multi-cloud-complexity/

Demand for DRAM for servers to exceed that for smartphones due to the growing use of cloud, AI, and HPC apps; DRAM content for servers forecast to increase by 12.1% YoY in 2023 compared to 6.7% for smartphones. Server memory will make up 37.6% of total DRAM bit output, up from 36.8% for mobile DRAM. COVID-19 pandemic has driven demand for cloud services, resulting in sharp increase in server shipments.

Cybersecurity

Cybersecurity company Resecurity has warned of a series of cyberattacks that have targeted data centers globally over the past 18 months, resulting in data exfiltration and publishing of access credentials on the dark web. Although Resecurity did not name the victims, Bloomberg claims that major corporations, including Alibaba, Amazon, Apple, BMW, Goldman Sachs, Huawei Technologies, Microsoft, and Walmart, had their data center credentials stolen. T

https://www.csoonline.com/article/3688909/cyberattacks-hit-data-centers-to-steal-information-from-global-companies.html#tk.rss_all

Cybersecurity firm Menlo Labs has uncovered an unknown threat actor group that is targeting government entities via a Discord-based campaign using the PureCrypter downloader. The campaign uses the domain of a compromised non-profit as a command and control hub to deliver a secondary payload, including the Redline Stealer, AgentTesla, Eternity, Blackmoon, and Philadelphia Ransomware.

https://www.menlosecurity.com/blog/purecrypter-targets-government-entities-through-discord

The biggest military cyber-warfare exercise in Western Europe occurred recently in Estonia, with 34 teams from 11 countries participating in a live-fire cyber battle. The seven-day event tested participants’ responses to common and complex cyber scenarios, including attacks on networks and industrial control systems (ICS). One scenario simulates attacks on uncrewed robotic systems. Teams from Italy, Estonia, and the UK were the top performers, judged based on their speed in identifying and responding to cyber threats.

https://www.securityweek.com/11-countries-take-part-in-military-cyberwarfare-exercise/

Embracing Digital Transformation Podcast

Check out this weeks full length episode "Certifying Autonomous Flight" where Darren interview LuukVan Dijk of Daedalean.

https://www.embracingdigital.org/episode-EDT126

briefs.summary: This Week at a Glance This week, we focus on critical developments in digital transformation that are shaping industry standards and practices. Staying informed about these developments is essential for organizations aiming to enhance their competiti...
briefs.content:
Artificial Intelligence

AI mistakes: Blame it on the inaccuracies in the input datasets.

  • Alphabet's shares dropped by $100 billion after Google's AI chatbot, Bard, shared inaccurate information in a promotional video, and a company event failed to impress. During a live event, Bard stumbled, prompting Google to pull the live stream, which fueled concerns that the tech giant is losing ground to its rival, Microsoft. Reuters reported that Bard credited the James Webb Space Telescope for taking the first pictures of a planet outside the solar system. In reality, the first pictures were taken by the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope. The incident highlights the importance of fact-checking before training AI models.

  • Not to be left behind Meta launched BlenderBot, a prototype conversational AI that soon told journalists it had deleted its Facebook account after learning about the company’s privacy scandals. “Since deleting Facebook my life has been much better,” it said. (oh oh)

  • In 2016 Microsoft apologized after a Twitter chatbot, Tay, started generating racist and sexist messages. It was forced to shut down the bot after users tweeted hateful remarks at Tay, which it then parroted. Its posts included likening feminism to cancer and suggesting the Holocaust did not happen.

Microsoft’s Satya Nadella told CNBC that AI-powered search is the biggest thing to happen to the company in the nine years he’s been CEO.

Otter.ai from FastCompany can automatically record meetings, take notes, and provide summaries, making it easier to track essential points. It can even perform these tasks over Zoom. https://www.fastcompany.com/90834773/how-to-use-ai-to-improve-employee-performance-and-engagement

Cybersecurity

New ESXiArgs Ransomware Variant Emerges After CISA Releases Decryptor Tool.

The threat actors behind the ESXiArgs ransomware attack have released an updated version that encrypts more data and removes the Bitcoin address from the ransom note, instead asking victims to contact them on Tox to obtain the wallet information. The new variant was reported by a system administrator, who said files larger than 128MB will have 50% of their data encrypted. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) had earlier released a decryptor to help affected victims recover from the attack. According to Censys, the attackers likely knew that the original encryption process was easy to circumvent and were aware that researchers were tracking their payments. https://thehackernews.com/2023/02/new-esxiargs-ransomware-variant-emerges.html

Microsoft, Google, and Apple are looking at replacing traditional passwords with secure passkeys to authenticate users. Passkeys, which offer greater security and resistance to phishing attempts, are becoming more popular as password security continues to be threatened by hackers. Internet security experts suggest that passkeys could become standard within a year, with companies such as Apple, Google, and Microsoft already pushing users towards using them. https://www.cnbc.com/2023/02/11/why-apple-google-microsoft-passkey-should-replace-your-own-password.html

Intelligent Edge

AT&T is collaborating with Ghost Robotics to use robotic dogs to improve public safety and national defense. The initiative will enhance the FirstNet emergency responder service, and network-connected robotic dogs can deliver a wide range of Internet of Things (IoT) use cases, including those that previously required putting personnel in dangerous situations. Lance Spencer, Client Executive VP - Defense at AT&T, said that this is one way to demonstrate the innovation and transformative possibilities of 5G and IoT. https://www.iottechnews.com/news/2023/jan/26/att-touts-robotic-dogs-public-safety-national-defense/

A study by Juniper Research predicts that the global number of 5G IoT connections will exceed 100 million by 2026, up 1,100% from 17 million connections in 2023. Healthcare and smart city services are expected to drive this growth. Over 60 million 5G smart city connections are expected globally. 5G will enable more efficient healthcare provision and IoT technologies can address healthcare inefficiencies exposed by the COVID-19 pandemic. Connected emergency services, telemedicine, and real-time remote monitoring will be the most useful applications of 5G IoT. https://www.iottechnews.com/news/2023/jan/24/5g-iot-connections-exceed-100m-by-2026/

briefs.summary: This Week at a Glance During the week of February 6, 2023, we witness significant developments in the fields of digital transformation, particularly focusing on artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and cybersecurity. These advancements are resha...
briefs.content:
Artificial Intelligence

According to Forbes, by 2030, AI will potentially deliver $13 trillion to the global economy, or 16% of the world's current GDP.

ChatGPT lets scammers craft emails that are so convincing they can get cash from victims without even relying on malware Some fear the powerful chatbot will make it far easier for non-coders to create malware and become cybercriminals

ChatGPT Cybersecurity Social Engineering

Google has invested almost $400 million in artificial intelligence startup Anthropic, which is testing a rival to OpenAI’s ChatGPT. https://interestingengineering.com/innovation/google-invests-anthropic-battle-chatgpt Google will be holding an event about how it’s “using the power of AI to reimagine how people search" A 40-minute event will be streamed on YouTube on February 8th at 8:30AM ET.

An AI detection tool, that checks for chatGPT written content, says Macbeth written by William Shakespeare was generated by AI. I guess chatGPT was not trained in Old English. Guess it was not trained on old English (aka Shakespearean English)

https://venturebeat.com/ai/chatgpt-detection-tool-thinks-macbeth-was-generated-by-ai-what-happens-now/

Ubiquitous Compute

Global public cloud revenues continue to increase, with the projected 26% growth to hit $525 billion this year, according to Statista. Software as a service is projected to be $253 Billion of that revenue. However, as the growth of the cloud continues, cloud services providers are feeling the pain, as there have been several outages over the last 12 months. This has been such a problem that multiple websites have popped up that monitor and report public cloud availability like cloudharmony.com and thousandeyes.com.

  • https://cloudharmony.com/status
  • https://www.thousandeyes.com/outages/
  • https://www.statista.com/outlook/tmo/public-cloud/worldwide

Oracle and Red Hat have teamed up to provide RHEL-based virtual machine instances in Oracle’s Cloud running on Intel, AMD, and Arm processors. This teaming between former competitors is providing customers with a one stop shop for workloads that utilize oracle’s suite of products and traditional linux based workloads. This move continues to push Oracle into competition with the big Hyper-scalers like Azure, AWS, and Google.

  • https://www.networkworld.com/article/3686513/red-hat-enterprise-linux-arrives-in-oracle-s-cloud.html

Cybersecurity

E-commerce in South Korea and the U.S. are being attacked by an ongoing GuLoader malware campaign, cybersecurity firm Trellix disclosed late last month. The cyber attackers are shifting away from Microsoft Word document approach to NSIS (Nullsoft Scriptable Install System) an open source tool for writing installers on the Windows Operating system.

GuLoader Malware Using Malicious NSIS

Pro-Russian hackers are using a new DDoS-as-a-Service Platform named Passion to target medical instituitons in the U. deepdives.content:
Can Leaders Govern AI as Cyber Risks Rise?

AI adoption is increasingly being decided by trust, while cyber resilience and network strategy are becoming core business issues rather than back-office concerns.

The central development this week is simple: digital transformation is still accelerating, but trust is now determining whether it succeeds. A fresh set of AI governance concerns, a visible rise in operational cyber risk, and renewed strategic attention to communications infrastructure all point to the same executive reality—leaders can no longer treat AI, security, and connectivity as separate agendas. They now define one another.

AI Is Powerful, but Governance Is the Gatekeeper

The most important signal in the AI market is not just what these tools can do, but how organizations control them. The OpenAI researcher firings over sensitive information breaches underscore a basic point: model capability is only part of the equation. Governance—meaning the rules, access controls, and oversight around a tool—can determine whether an AI program builds trust or creates new harm.

There is also a branding and adoption problem. When employees and customers hear “AI” and assume replacement rather than augmentation, resistance starts before value is demonstrated. That makes executive framing matter. Successful adoption is more likely when leaders connect AI to a specific workflow, a specific data set, and a specific human outcome, rather than presenting it as a broad transformation campaign.

Cyber Risk Is No Longer Just an IT Problem

The week’s cyber incidents show that security failures now hit the business itself, not just the technical environment. The Intermarché attack is a reminder that retail disruption can affect payments, logistics, and customer trust at the same time. The iRhythm breach points in the same direction: in healthcare and other regulated sectors, cyber incidents quickly become operational, reputational, and privacy issues.

That is why resilience has become an operating requirement. Detection and response still matter, but so do recovery planning, employee training, and coordination across functions. A strong security posture is no longer just a defensive cost. It is part of the conditions required for digital transformation to work at all.

Connectivity Is Becoming Strategic Infrastructure

The FCC’s spectrum move, SpaceX’s carrier ambitions, and open network efforts all point to a communications environment that is becoming more flexible and more contested. The strategic question for enterprises is no longer simply whether they have connectivity, but what kind of connectivity they can depend on, scale with, and recover through.

That matters because AI tools, cloud workflows, and field operations all depend on reliable access. Hybrid network models can reduce lock-in and increase adaptability, but they also require stronger integration discipline. For executives, connectivity is now a platform decision, not a utility purchase.

What Executives Should Do Now

For CIOs, the practical move is to tie AI to workflow value, not broad experimentation. A narrow, private deployment with clear boundaries is more likely to succeed than a public, open-ended pilot. The example of a controlled use case in a court clerk setting reflects the right logic: start with one workflow, one data set, and one measurable outcome.

For CISOs, the key assumption should be that every new digital service expands the attack surface. If data access is weak, automation multiplies exposure. That means stronger identity controls, tighter vendor review, and better employee training need to sit alongside AI and cloud initiatives.

For government leaders and other organizations in regulated environments, the message is balance rather than blanket resistance. Public skepticism is real, but the answer is to govern well: private generative AI, clear retention rules, redaction, and human review can deliver efficiency without sacrificing accountability. Control has to come first if trust is going to follow.

The Main Risks to Watch

The first risk is backlash. If workers and stakeholders hear only job loss and not augmentation, adoption can stall before value is proven. Technology alone cannot fix a cultural rejection of change.

The second is weak data control. AI is only as safe as the permissions and data around it. If those are exposed, the tool can scale the problem instead of solving it.

The third is network dependency. As hybrid connectivity becomes more central, outages or vendor friction can turn into single points of failure for logistics, field work, customer service, and safety-critical operations.

What leaders can take forward

The lesson for leaders is that trust has become the new adoption gate. Cyber resilience is now part of transformation, not a separate discipline, and connectivity is emerging as strategic infrastructure rather than background plumbing. Organizations that move fastest will not be the ones that experiment the most, but the ones that accelerate with control, discipline, and a clear human outcome in view.

2026-10-5 | AI Governance, Cybersecurity & Space Data | Embracing Digital This Week

AI governance, cybersecurity and even space-based data centers are moving from speculative discussion to practical deployment, forcing executives to rethink oversight, resilience and infrastructure planning.

The central story is not that AI, cyber risk and space infrastructure are changing separately, but that they are converging into a single management challenge for business and government leaders. AI governance is moving from debate to implementation, cybersecurity is being treated as a board-level operational risk, and technology firms are beginning to explore orbital data centers to support growing AI demand. Together, these shifts matter because they change how organizations must think about accountability, resilience and the physical limits of digital growth.

AI governance is moving from concern to control

One of the clearest developments is the shift in AI governance from broad concern to active oversight. A new task force is examining risks, signaling that policymakers are no longer treating AI as an abstract future issue. Instead, they are beginning to shape the next phase of AI use through deliberate governance structures.

That shift is reinforced by efforts to test major AI models for bias, accuracy and accountability. The practical implication is straightforward: companies can no longer rely on performance alone when evaluating AI systems. They must also be able to show how those systems are supervised, how human judgment is retained, and how outputs are checked before they influence decisions.

Trust, bias and human oversight are now business issues

The analysis points to a growing emphasis on trust as a competitive and regulatory issue. As AI systems become more embedded in business processes, questions about bias and accountability become harder to separate from ordinary operations. A model that is fast or capable but opaque can create downstream risk in hiring, customer service, compliance or public messaging.

For executives, the practical lesson is that AI governance is no longer only a legal or technical function. It is an operating discipline. Organizations need clear oversight roles, review processes for high-impact use cases, and a way to explain how human oversight works in practice. The more AI influences decision-making, the more important those controls become.

AI is also changing how work is organized

Another major shift is the way AI tools are changing team structure and productivity expectations. The deep-dive notes that one person can now do the work of a small team in some contexts, which is already affecting hiring plans and productivity goals. That does not mean organizations can simply cut staff and expect the same results. It does mean the definition of output is changing.

This has strategic consequences. Leaders may need to rethink workforce planning, role design and performance metrics. If AI makes certain tasks faster or easier, then businesses will need to decide whether the goal is to reduce headcount, increase throughput, improve quality or redirect staff toward higher-value work. Those choices are managerial, not just technological.

Cybersecurity is becoming more adaptive and more public

Cybersecurity is also shifting from static defenses to AI-powered resilience strategies. The analysis describes a move toward adaptive defense, which means security tools are increasingly expected to detect unusual behavior, respond faster and adjust to changing threats. This reflects a wider recognition that traditional perimeter-based security is no longer enough on its own.

The Citrix attack underscores another important point: cyber risk is not just an IT matter. It is an operational and reputational issue that reaches the boardroom. When critical systems are exposed, the consequences can include business interruption, customer concern and loss of trust. That is why cyber preparedness now needs to be treated as part of enterprise risk management, not simply as a technical safeguard.

Awareness and resilience now extend beyond the enterprise

The episode also suggests that public cyber awareness is becoming part of resilience strategy. That matters because cybersecurity failures do not stop at the edge of an organization; they affect employees, customers and the wider public. If states and institutions are helping people understand cyber risks, they are effectively strengthening the broader environment in which companies operate.

For executives, this broadens the action list. Security teams still need strong defenses, but organizations also need incident planning, communication protocols and executive-level accountability. In a world where cyber events quickly become public events, the response can matter as much as the breach itself.

Space data centers show how far AI infrastructure is stretching

Perhaps the most forward-looking development is the push toward orbital data centers. Tech firms are exploring space-based infrastructure to meet AI workload demands and reduce pressure on terrestrial power grids. In plain terms, companies are looking beyond Earth because conventional infrastructure is coming under strain from the scale of AI computing needs.

This is significant not because orbital computing is mainstream today, but because it shows how far infrastructure planning is being pushed by AI growth. It also raises policy questions. The pace of innovation appears to be outstripping the ability of regulators to keep up, especially when infrastructure moves into a new physical and legal environment. That creates uncertainty around governance, security and standards.

What leaders can take forward

The common thread across AI governance, cybersecurity and space data is that digital transformation is becoming more consequential, more regulated and more physical. Leaders should assume that oversight, resilience and infrastructure planning will need to evolve together. The organizations that respond earliest will be better positioned to manage risk, sustain trust and make practical use of new technologies as they mature.

2026-9-21 | AI Governance, Cybersecurity & Cloud Risk | Embracing Digital This Week

AI governance is moving from policy debate to practical oversight, while cybersecurity and cloud strategy are being reshaped by real-world AI risk and rising demand for resilient digital infrastructure.

AI governance, cybersecurity, and cloud risk are converging into one board-level issue: how to adopt AI without exposing the business to regulatory, operational, and infrastructure failures. The latest analysis shows Washington moving toward stronger AI oversight, cyber threats shifting from abstract concerns to live enterprise risks, and cloud architectures being tested by the scale of AI demand. For executives, the message is clear: resilience, governance, and adaptability are no longer side projects; they are core requirements for growth.

Washington Is Moving From AI Debate to Oversight

The central policy development is a sharper AI agenda from the White House, alongside regulators and lawmakers weighing stronger oversight. The significance is not just political symbolism. It suggests that AI governance is moving beyond broad discussion and into action, where organizations may face more concrete expectations around safety, accountability, and market behavior.

For business leaders, this means AI strategy can no longer be treated as a purely technical or experimental matter. Companies need governance structures that can keep up with changing rules, including internal review processes, clearer accountability for AI use, and documentation that can withstand scrutiny. The analysis also points to a competitive reality: organizations that build credible and adaptable AI programs are likely to be better positioned than those relying on bold claims alone.

Cyber Risk Is No Longer Theoretical

A second major shift is that AI-related cyber risk is now showing up in real companies and critical systems, not just in research labs or hypothetical scenarios. That matters because it moves the risk discussion from possibility to operational reality. AI can be used to sharpen attacks, expand the scale of malicious activity, and complicate defense efforts for organizations that depend on digital systems.

At the same time, cybersecurity guidance is changing. The analysis describes a move toward low-cost controls and better coordination across sectors, which indicates a more practical and governance-driven model of defense. Rather than assuming security can be solved by adding more tools, the emphasis is on disciplined oversight, shared responsibility, and coordinated response. For executives, that means cybersecurity programs should be judged not only by detection technology, but by whether the organization can make decisions quickly, align across functions, and reduce exposure in a measurable way.

Cloud Architecture Must Absorb Disruption

The cloud and digital infrastructure discussion is being reshaped by surging demand for AI capability. The analysis argues that digital growth now depends on architectures that can absorb disruption, not just add capacity. In plain terms, it is no longer enough for systems to handle more traffic or more workloads; they also need to keep operating when demand spikes, supply constraints appear, or dependencies fail.

This is where cloud risk becomes a strategic issue rather than a purely technical one. As AI adoption increases, organizations may discover that their current architecture is efficient but brittle. That creates pressure to examine redundancy, portability, dependency management, and the ability to recover quickly from disruption. The practical takeaway is that infrastructure planning should be tied to business continuity, not just performance targets. Leaders should ask whether their digital environment can scale without becoming more fragile.

Why Governance Now Matters Across The Stack

One of the strongest themes in the analysis is that governance is becoming the common thread across AI, cyber, and cloud. In all three areas, the issue is not just innovation, but control: who decides, who is accountable, and how risk is managed when conditions change quickly. That is why the material emphasizes a shift from tools to governance in cybersecurity and from theory to action in AI oversight.

For executives, this means technology decisions should be paired with operating-model changes. Boards and leadership teams need clearer ownership of AI policy, cyber resilience, and infrastructure risk. They also need mechanisms that allow the business to adapt as rules, economics, and technical requirements keep shifting. The organizations that can do this well will likely move faster and with less friction than those that treat each domain as a separate challenge.

The Practical Executive Response

The most useful response is not to wait for perfect clarity. Instead, organizations should strengthen the basics that support adaptability: define AI governance responsibilities, review cyber controls with an emphasis on coordination and simplicity, and test whether cloud architecture can tolerate disruption as AI demand rises. These steps are consistent with the analysis’ core point that resilience is becoming a business advantage.

Executives should also be careful about the gap between claims and capability. If AI is part of the growth plan, leadership needs evidence that the organization can support it safely and sustainably. That includes transparent governance, realistic risk management, and digital infrastructure that can flex as conditions change. In that sense, the challenge is not merely to adopt more technology, but to build an organization that can absorb technological change without losing control.

What leaders can take forward

AI governance, cybersecurity, and cloud risk are no longer separate conversations. The policy environment is tightening, cyber threats are becoming more operational, and AI demand is exposing weaknesses in digital architecture. The organizations most likely to succeed will be those that treat governance and resilience as strategic capabilities, not compliance afterthoughts.

2026-9-14 | Responsible AI: Trust, Risk, and Governance | Embracing Digital This Week

Responsible AI is moving from a technical ambition to a board-level discipline, with leaders now balancing innovation, security, governance, and human judgment as AI spreads through the enterprise.

The central development in AI right now is not just faster adoption, but a sharper demand for control. Across industry and policy, organizations are being pushed to prove that AI systems are safe, accountable, and aligned with human judgment before they scale them broadly. That matters because the companies that treat governance as an afterthought are likely to face greater security, regulatory, and trust risks as AI becomes embedded in everyday work.

Why governance is becoming a prerequisite for AI scale

A recurring theme is that AI deployment needs more discipline before it needs more speed. One clear signal comes from Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, who has argued that the industry may need to slow down and focus on safety. The practical meaning for enterprises is straightforward: if AI is going to influence decisions, workflows, and customer interactions, leaders need policies for how systems are approved, monitored, and updated.

This is not just a technical issue. AI use is increasingly a workplace and policy concern, which means companies are under pressure to demonstrate accountability. That includes being able to explain where AI is used, who is responsible for its outputs, and what controls exist when systems fail or behave unexpectedly. Governance is becoming the foundation for trust, not a compliance afterthought.

Security risks are rising alongside AI adoption

AI is also changing the security conversation. The analysis points to stronger scrutiny of AI systems as leaders respond to vulnerabilities and the possibility of new attack paths. In boardrooms, AI security is being treated as a priority because innovation without controls can widen exposure rather than reduce it.

Europe’s response underscores the point. The region is pushing harder on cyber resilience as AI expands the attack surface. In plain terms, that means more systems, more data, and more opportunities for misuse or compromise. For executives, the lesson is that AI programs should be designed with security from the start, including access controls, monitoring, and clear boundaries around sensitive data and model use.

Geopolitics and sovereign AI are shaping strategy

The AI race is also strategic, not just commercial. China is sharpening its AI strategy to reduce dependence on U.S. technology and influence international standards. That puts pressure on global companies to think carefully about supply chains, infrastructure choices, and the long-term implications of platform dependence.

This is where the idea of sovereign AI enters the picture. The analysis ties AI adoption to data control, governance, and accountability, suggesting that organizations want more control over how data is stored, accessed, and used. For enterprises operating across regions, that means technology decisions are increasingly tied to regulatory exposure, resilience, and strategic autonomy. Executives should view sovereignty as a business planning issue, not only a national policy issue.

Human judgment remains central to responsible AI

A key principle in the discussion is that AI should strengthen human judgment and empathy, not replace them. That framing matters because it moves the conversation away from automation for its own sake and toward augmentation: using AI to support decisions while preserving human oversight where nuance, ethics, and context matter.

This is especially important in organizations where decisions affect customers, employees, or critical operations. AI can accelerate analysis and surface patterns, but it does not remove the need for people who can interpret context, challenge outputs, and apply judgment. The practical takeaway for leaders is to define where AI can recommend and where humans must decide. That boundary is central to responsible adoption.

What executives should do now

The combined message is that responsible AI requires operating discipline. Executives should establish governance before broad deployment, strengthen security review for AI tools and data flows, and make accountability explicit across teams. They should also ensure that AI programs are designed to preserve human oversight, especially in high-stakes processes.

In addition, leaders should treat data control as a strategic requirement and not simply a technical preference. That means asking where data resides, who can access it, how outputs are validated, and how quickly controls can adapt as regulations and threats evolve. Organizations that build these foundations early are more likely to scale AI with confidence rather than react under pressure.

What leaders can take forward

The direction of travel is clear: AI is becoming more powerful, but also more governed. The organizations best positioned to benefit will be those that pair innovation with security, accountability, and human judgment. Responsible AI is no longer a future discussion; it is now a practical requirement for trust, resilience, and long-term competitiveness.

2026-9-7 | Hidden Flaws in AI & Cybersecurity | Embracing Digital This Week

AI is shifting from novelty to operational discipline, with enterprises prioritizing reliability, open-source flexibility, and stronger cyber hygiene as threats and infrastructure demands evolve.

The latest turn in enterprise technology is not another sprint for flashy AI features, but a harder conversation about control, consistency, and resilience. Across AI and cybersecurity, the signal is clear: organizations are running into the practical limits of fast deployment, while attackers are getting more capable and infrastructure leaders are preparing for a more demanding connectivity future. For executives, that means innovation now has to be judged not only by what it can do, but by how reliably it works, how well it can be governed, and how securely it fits into the business.

AI is running into the limits of speed

One of the strongest themes is that the AI race is hitting a practical wall. The issue is not whether progress continues, but whether systems perform consistently enough to be trusted in day-to-day business use. That matters because organizations increasingly want reliability over novelty: models need to behave predictably, work across contexts, and produce outputs that can be governed.

This is a meaningful shift in how executives should think about AI investment. Early enthusiasm often centered on capability demonstrations and rapid feature release. The current reality is more demanding. If a system produces inconsistent results, the cost shows up in rework, human oversight, and loss of confidence from users and customers. The business case now depends as much on operational quality as on technical sophistication.

Open-source AI is becoming a strategic choice

Another important development is the rise of open-source AI as a serious business option. Rather than defaulting to closed, proprietary platforms, organizations are increasingly weighing flexibility, control, and lower lock-in. That does not mean open source is automatically better for every use case, but it does mean it is no longer a fringe choice.

For enterprises, the appeal is strategic. Open-source approaches can offer more room to adapt models to specific needs and to avoid dependence on a single vendor’s roadmap. In practice, that can help teams build a more tailored AI stack and manage long-term costs or integration constraints. The challenge is that flexibility also brings responsibility: organizations still need strong governance, model oversight, and integration discipline to make open source workable at scale.

Cybersecurity is moving from reactive to built-in

The cybersecurity picture in the analysis is blunt: security gaps can still emerge in mature environments, and recent breaches involving well-known organizations underline that no environment is immune. The lesson is not simply that breaches happen, but that defensive maturity cannot be assumed just because an organization is established or technically sophisticated.

That is pushing more companies toward proactive security design. Instead of treating security as something applied after deployment or after an incident, the emphasis is increasingly on building protections into systems from the start. This is especially important as AI changes the threat landscape. The NSA warning highlighted in the analysis reinforces a basic point that remains true even in a more advanced environment: good cyber hygiene still matters. Patch discipline, access control, user awareness, and routine security practices remain foundational, particularly when attackers can use AI to target victims more precisely.

AI is also becoming part of the defense stack

The same technology driving new risks is also being used to improve defense. Nvidia and CrowdStrike are among the companies developing new AI models for cybersecurity with the goal of speeding threat response. The significance here is not that AI replaces security teams, but that it can help them move faster when the volume and complexity of alerts exceed what humans can process alone.

This points to a broader operational reality. AI is moving from an experimental layer to infrastructure inside cybersecurity workflows. That can improve detection, triage, and response, but only if the tools themselves are resilient and well tuned. Executives should be cautious about assuming that AI-based security systems are automatically smarter or safer. Like any critical platform, they need monitoring, testing, and clear human judgment around when to trust automation and when to override it.

Connectivity strategy is being reset for resilience

Beyond AI and cyber, the analysis notes a parallel upgrade in satellite communications, with a focus on stronger security and resilience in contested environments. That matters because communications infrastructure is becoming a strategic issue, not just a technical one. The trend is toward data links that can withstand disruption and support more dependable operations.

The forward-looking recommendation is straightforward: organizations should build flexible connectivity now to prepare for a 6G-ready future. The deeper point is that digital transformation cannot be treated as a sequence of isolated upgrades. Connectivity, governance, standards, and security all have to evolve together. For leaders, that means planning infrastructure with enough adaptability to absorb new network capabilities without forcing repeated redesigns.

What leaders can take forward

Taken together, these developments suggest a more mature phase of digital transformation. AI is no longer just about what can be generated; it is about what can be controlled, trusted, and integrated responsibly. Cybersecurity is shifting toward prevention and resilience rather than post-incident repair, and communications strategy is increasingly tied to security and future readiness. The executives who respond best will be the ones who pair innovation with governance, choose flexibility without sacrificing control, and treat reliability as a core technology requirement rather than a nice-to-have.

2026-8-31 | AI at Work: Skills, Security, Robots | Embracing Digital This Week

AI is moving from experimental pilots into day-to-day operations, while cybersecurity, workforce skills, and robotics are becoming the central issues leaders must manage at the same time.

Artificial intelligence is no longer confined to labs or isolated pilots. Across business, security, education, and robotics, the technology is moving into real workflows and public life, forcing leaders to confront a new set of practical questions: how to govern AI use, how to defend against AI-amplified threats, and how to prepare people and systems for faster change. The central message is not that AI is arriving someday, but that it is already reshaping operations and risk management now.

AI Is Moving Closer to Core Operations

One of the clearest developments is the rise of forward-deployed AI, where companies are pushing models into real workflows rather than treating them as side projects. That shift matters because it changes AI from a concept demo into an operational tool that must deliver usable output, fit business processes, and be managed at scale.

At the same time, AI tools are reaching a broader audience. Access is expanding through national programs and through everyday creative work, which suggests demand is spreading beyond specialized technical teams. The practical implication for executives is straightforward: broad access without governance can create inconsistency, but broad access with training and clear controls can unlock more value.

Why Governance and Training Now Matter More

As AI becomes more widely available, organizations need to pay more attention to how people use it and what standards guide that use. The challenge is not only whether the tool works, but whether the output is reliable, usable, and appropriate for the task at hand. That makes governance and training central enablers, not optional extras.

Leaders should treat AI adoption as an operating-model change. If employees are expected to use AI in daily work, then policies, oversight, and skills development need to scale with that expectation. Without that foundation, companies risk inconsistent results and weak value capture even when the technology itself is capable.

Cybersecurity Pressure Is Rising Alongside AI

AI is also amplifying cybersecurity concerns at a time when major breaches continue to surface. That combination is important: the same broad access and automation that can improve productivity can also help attackers move faster and adapt more quickly.

Ransomware groups are already adopting newer development tools, which gives them speed and flexibility. In plain terms, attackers are not standing still. They are using better tooling to make their operations more efficient, which raises the stakes for defenders. For organizations, this means security teams need to assume that adversaries will increasingly use AI-enabled methods to scale attacks, refine payloads, and respond faster to defenses.

The lesson for executives is to connect AI strategy with security strategy. Expanding AI use inside the enterprise without strengthening protection for data, identities, and systems increases exposure. The more AI touches business-critical information, the more important it becomes to control what data is accessible, who can use it, and how it is monitored.

Building the Cyber Skills Pipeline

The response to growing cyber risk cannot come from enterprises alone. Fortinet’s free cybersecurity curriculum for U.S. high schools points to a wider effort to address the talent gap earlier in the education pipeline. That matters because the cybersecurity skills shortage is not just an enterprise staffing issue; it is a long-term workforce issue.

This kind of program suggests a more proactive model: rather than waiting until workers enter the job market, organizations and education providers are starting to build foundational cyber awareness sooner. For business leaders, the practical takeaway is that workforce resilience depends on more than hiring. It also depends on partnerships, training pathways, and investments that expand the future supply of security talent.

Robots Are Becoming Part of the Enterprise Fabric

Robotics is also moving deeper into the enterprise. The trend is no longer just about automation in isolated settings; it is increasingly about robots becoming part of core operations. That shift signals that firms are looking beyond efficiency gains and toward systems that can work alongside existing processes more directly.

There is also evidence of a move toward shared workflows rather than automation alone. Human-robot collaboration changes the design problem: organizations must think about how people and machines coordinate, how responsibilities are divided, and how work is supervised. This is especially relevant for leaders evaluating robotics investments, because the value comes not just from replacing tasks, but from redesigning work in a way that makes human and machine capabilities complementary.

Market signals from China reinforce the point that demand for AI and robotics is accelerating. For global executives, that suggests the competitive landscape is tightening. If major markets are moving quickly, firms elsewhere may need to accelerate their own experimentation and capability-building to avoid falling behind.

What Leaders Should Do Next

The combined signal across AI, security, and robotics is that digital transformation is becoming more integrated and more consequential. Leaders should focus on three priorities: strengthen governance, invest in workforce readiness, and align technology adoption with security requirements. These are not separate initiatives; they are linked parts of the same transition.

In practical terms, that means setting clear rules for AI use, training employees to use tools effectively, and ensuring security teams have the visibility and controls needed to defend against faster-moving threats. It also means thinking beyond pilots and asking how AI and robotics will change everyday operations, not just isolated functions.

What leaders can take forward

AI is now influencing how organizations work, how attackers operate, and how the next generation of skills is developed. The companies that benefit most will be the ones that treat adoption, security, and workforce planning as one connected agenda rather than three separate problems.

AI is moving from pilots into everyday healthcare work, but the next phase of digital transformation will depend on stronger cybersecurity, clearer regulation, and real evidence that connected tools improve patient care.

Artificial intelligence is no longer confined to healthcare experiments: it is increasingly being woven into everyday clinical work, from creating and maintaining medical records to supporting decision-making. That shift matters because it raises the stakes for cybersecurity, regulatory compliance, and proof of patient benefit. For healthcare leaders, the challenge is no longer whether to adopt digital tools, but how to do so quickly without undermining trust, safety, or operational resilience.

AI is entering routine clinical workflows

The most important change is that AI is moving from pilot projects into daily healthcare operations. Tools are now helping with core administrative and clinical tasks, including the creation and maintenance of medical records. That signals a broader shift: AI is becoming part of the workflow, not just an adjacent support layer.

For executives, this means AI strategy can no longer sit solely with innovation teams or technical specialists. When AI touches records, scheduling, documentation, or decision support, it affects governance, staffing, training, liability, and the patient experience. Leaders need a clear view of where AI is being used, who oversees it, and how its outputs are validated before they are trusted in practice.

Cybersecurity is now a board-level healthcare issue

As more patient data moves through digital systems, the consequences of a breach become more severe. The underlying risk is not abstract: attacks can expose patient data, genetic records, and medical systems. That broadens cybersecurity from a back-office concern to a direct patient-safety and trust issue.

The pressure is especially acute for rural providers, which often have less budget and fewer staff to harden their defenses. That makes them more vulnerable to disruption and harder-hit by the costs of recovery. The practical implication is that security strategy must be scaled to organizational reality, not built on assumptions that every provider has the same resources. Boards and executives should prioritize basic resilience, incident response, and vendor oversight alongside any AI deployment.

Connected devices are expanding the attack surface

Connected medical devices are becoming more deeply embedded in care delivery, and that creates both clinical opportunity and operational risk. When devices are networked, software-driven, or able to act with increasing autonomy, they are no longer isolated equipment. They become part of a larger digital environment that must be secured, monitored, and maintained.

This is why executive teams need to treat device strategy as part of enterprise digital transformation, not as a separate biomedical or IT procurement issue. Every connected device adds a potential entry point, data source, and compliance obligation. The more care depends on these systems, the more important it becomes to understand how they are patched, monitored, authenticated, and integrated with broader security controls.

Autonomy is advancing faster than evidence

Regulators are authorizing more autonomous medical technology, which suggests growing confidence in these tools and in the frameworks used to evaluate them. But authorization is not the same as demonstrating broad clinical value in real-world settings. A key concern is that many AI-cleared medical devices still lack strong evidence of patient benefit.

That distinction matters for leaders deciding where to invest and what to scale. Faster approval can accelerate access to innovation, but organizations still need to ask whether a product improves outcomes, reduces workload, or meaningfully changes care. In practice, executives should demand evidence that goes beyond technical performance and addresses patient benefit, workflow impact, and safety in deployment. Otherwise, organizations risk adopting tools that are permitted but not yet proven to deliver durable value.

What leaders should do next

The episode’s central message is that healthcare digital transformation is now a three-part balancing act: speed, security, and proof. AI is advancing quickly into workflows, but the organizations that benefit most will be those that match adoption with disciplined cybersecurity and a strong evidentiary standard for clinical value.

For executives, the action list is straightforward. Inventory where AI and connected devices are already in use. Strengthen cyber controls around patient data and medical systems, especially where resources are limited. Make governance explicit so that clinical, technical, and compliance teams share responsibility. And before scaling new AI tools, require clear evidence of patient benefit, not just vendor claims or regulatory clearance. That approach will help build trust with clinicians, patients, and regulators while reducing the risk that speed outpaces safety.

What leaders can take forward

Healthcare is entering a phase where AI, cybersecurity, and connected devices are converging in the same operating environment. The organizations most likely to succeed will be those that treat AI as a leadership issue, not just a technology trend, and that pair adoption with security discipline and measurable proof of patient benefit.

2026-8-17 | AI Trust, Cyber Risk & Cloud Resilience | Embracing Digital This Week

AI trust, cyber defense, and cloud resilience are converging as organizations face faster adoption, stricter safeguards, and greater pressure to prove their systems are reliable.

AI is moving quickly from novelty to everyday business tool, but the supporting trust, security, and resilience layers are not keeping pace automatically. The result is a more demanding digital environment: organizations now have to verify AI-generated content, strengthen cyber defenses, and plan for cloud failures or provider disruption at the same time. For executives, the message is clear—digital transformation is no longer just about adoption speed, but about building systems that can be trusted under real-world pressure.

AI adoption is forcing trust to become a technical requirement

One of the clearest developments is the effort to add safeguards to AI-generated text. Anthropic has introduced watermarking for Claude’s output, a step aimed at making machine-written content easier to identify. That matters because text generation is spreading faster than trust, and organizations increasingly need ways to tell what was created by people and what was created by systems.

The broader workplace implication is that AI fluency is moving from optional to expected. That does not mean every role needs deep technical expertise, but it does mean organizations should treat AI literacy as a hiring and training issue. The practical challenge is not just using AI tools, but understanding where they are reliable, where they are not, and how to verify their outputs before they influence business decisions or public communication.

Governance and guardrails are becoming part of digital operations

The episode’s analysis points to a larger truth: digital systems need guardrails to stay reliable. AI can accelerate prototyping, onboarding, and knowledge sharing, but production-ready systems still require architecture, testing, human judgment, and trust. In other words, speed is valuable only when it is paired with control.

For executives, this means governance cannot be an afterthought. AI deployment should include clear approval paths, content review processes, and defined accountability for errors. Where AI is used to support operational decisions, teams need to know when to accept machine output and when to require human review. The immediate goal is not to block innovation, but to reduce the risk of deploying systems that look effective in demos but fail under operational pressure.

Cybersecurity is shifting from reactive defense to coordinated resilience

Cyber risk is intensifying across sectors, and the response is becoming more structured. California will give each state agency an AI cybersecurity officer, signaling that AI-related risk is now being treated as a formal governance issue rather than a side concern. At the same time, Cisco firewall vulnerabilities have put network teams on alert after issues disrupted VPN services, underscoring how quickly a software flaw can affect core access and connectivity.

The cyber picture is also changing strategically. More private companies are exploring offensive cyber operations as criminal gangs increase attacks. That does not mean every company should move in that direction, but it does show how defensive thinking is evolving. Organizations are being pushed to understand threat actor behavior more deeply, invest in faster patching discipline, and coordinate security decisions across IT, legal, and executive leadership.

Cloud convenience is colliding with the cost of overdependence

Cloud growth continues across government and industry, but recent events are exposing a downside that often gets overlooked: dependence on a single provider can become a business continuity risk. A PBS station is now scrambling after a cloud provider vanished, putting 50 terabytes of media at risk. That is a concrete reminder that cloud services are useful only as long as they remain accessible, recoverable, and contractually supported.

The lesson for organizations is straightforward. Cloud strategy should not stop at migration; it must include contingency planning. Leaders should know where critical data resides, how quickly it can be restored, and what happens if a provider changes terms, fails, or disappears. Backup architecture, exit planning, and data portability are no longer niche technical concerns. They are central to resilience planning.

What executives should do now

The common thread across AI, cybersecurity, and cloud resilience is verification. Whether the issue is AI-generated content, network security, or data storage, organizations need systems that can be trusted before they scale. That requires policies, technical controls, and clear ownership—not just enthusiasm for digital transformation.

Executives should focus on three actions: first, build AI governance that includes content verification and human review; second, treat cybersecurity as an enterprise risk function tied to leadership oversight and rapid patching discipline; and third, reduce cloud concentration risk by testing backups, recovery procedures, and provider exit options. The organizations most likely to succeed will be the ones that pair adoption with resilience.

What leaders can take forward

The digital landscape is no longer defined only by innovation speed. It is defined by whether organizations can prove their tools, protect their systems, and recover when dependencies fail. AI, cyber risk, and cloud resilience are now tightly connected, and executives who address them together will be better positioned to move fast without losing control.
